passage.title: A Whistle Across the Pasture
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Morning dew still clung to the clover in the north pasture when Eli unlatched the wooden gate. Beside his boots, Pip, a ten-month-old border collie with black-and-white fur, quivered like a coiled spring. All week, Eli had tried to help his grandfather move the flock of twenty ewes from the hill down to the wooden pen. Yet every time Pip sprinted toward the sheep, Eli had shouted and waved his arms to steer the puppy. Instead of listening, Pip had barked wildly and scattered the wooly flock into the briars.

Grandfather walked over and handed Eli a flat silver shepherd's whistle strung on a leather cord. He explained that a loud human voice sounds like panic to both a young dog and nervous sheep. The nervous ewes near the stone wall, startled earlier by Eli's waving arms and loud shouts, were calmly gathered by Grandfather's older dog with a wide, silent sweep. Pip watched the older dog glide along the edge of the flock without making a single yip.

Eli pressed the curved metal whistle against his tongue and blew a soft, low note. Grandfather had taught him two basic signals on the porch after supper. One long, steady blast told the dog to lie flat in the grass and pause. Two short, rising notes told the dog to circle wide to the left around the flock. Because a clear whistle cuts through valley wind without sounding angry, a working dog can hear the cue from half a mile away.

When Grandfather nodded, Eli sent Pip trotting up the green slope toward the grazing ewes. Halfway up the hill, the puppy lowered his head and sped up, ready to charge straight into the middle of the sheep. Eli resisted the urge to yell across the grass. Instead, he blew one firm, level note on the silver whistle.

Pip's ears twitched, and his belly dropped straight into the wet clover. The ewes merely lifted their heads without bolting. After a three-second pause, Eli blew two crisp rising notes. Pip rose smoothly and trotted in a wide arc around the left flank, guiding the whole flock straight through the open gate.

tier2Words.definition: trembled or shook slightly with excitement or eagerness
tier2Words.rootHint: From Middle English quiver, meaning 'nimble, eager, or trembling'
tier2Words.contextClue: Beside Eli's boots, the eager border collie puppy trembled like a coiled spring waiting to run.

tier2Words.definition: drove or sent off in many different directions
tier2Words.rootHint: From Middle English scateren, meaning 'to separate and dash apart'
tier2Words.contextClue: When Pip barked wildly, the frightened flock broke apart and ran into the briars.

tier2Words.definition: held back from doing something even when tempted
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root sistere ('to stand firm') + prefix re- ('against')
tier2Words.contextClue: Instead of yelling across the grass when Pip sped up, Eli held back and used his whistle.

tier2Words.definition: the side edge of a group, herd, or body
tier2Words.contextClue: Following the two-note signal to circle left, Pip trotted in a wide arc around the left side of the flock.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"The nervous ewes near the stone wall, startled earlier by Eli's waving arms and loud shouts, were calmly gathered by Grandfather's older dog with a wide, silent sweep."

Based on the sentence, what startled the ewes earlier, and what gathered them calmly?

options.text: Grandfather's older dog startled the ewes near the wall, and Eli's loud shouts gathered them into the pen.
options.childFeedback: This swaps the two causes! Eli's loud shouts and waving arms are what startled the sheep, while Grandfather's older dog calmly gathered them with a silent sweep.

options.text: The stone wall gathered Eli's waving arms while the nervous ewes chased the older dog.
options.childFeedback: A stone wall cannot gather waving arms, and the nervous ewes were not chasing the dog!

options.text: Eli's waving arms and loud shouts startled the ewes, and Grandfather's older dog calmly gathered them.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, 'startled earlier by Eli's waving arms and loud shouts' and 'were calmly gathered by Grandfather's older dog' show that Eli's waving arms and shouts startled the ewes, and Grandfather's older dog calmly gathered them.

options.text: A sudden clap of thunder startled the flock, and a farm truck herded them down the hill.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 says morning dew clung to the clover on a calm morning—there was no thunder or farm truck in the pasture.

questions.provingSentenceText: The nervous ewes near the stone wall, startled earlier by Eli's waving arms and loud shouts, were calmly gathered by Grandfather's older dog with a wide, silent sweep.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, 'startled earlier by Eli's waving arms and loud shouts' and 'were calmly gathered by Grandfather's older dog' show that Eli's waving arms and shouts startled the ewes, and Grandfather's older dog calmly gathered them.
questions.parentExplanation: This passive sentence contains two 'by' phrases: 'startled earlier by Eli's waving arms and loud shouts' and 'were calmly gathered by Grandfather's older dog'. Option B tracks both accurately.
questions.retryHint: Look at the two 'by' phrases in Paragraph 2: 'startled earlier by...' and 'were calmly gathered by...'

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 4:

"Halfway up the hill, the puppy lowered his head and sped up, ready to charge straight into the middle of the sheep. Eli resisted the urge to yell across the grass. Instead, he blew one firm, level note on the silver whistle."

What does the word resisted mean as it is used in Paragraph 4?

options.text: Stopped himself from doing something he felt like doing
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'resisted' means stopped himself from doing something he felt like doing, because instead of yelling when Pip sped up, Eli held back and blew one firm note on the whistle.

options.text: Shouted as loudly as possible across the pasture
options.childFeedback: Shouting across the pasture is what Eli used to do in Paragraph 1; in Paragraph 4, he 'resisted the urge to yell' and used the whistle instead.

options.text: Forgot which whistle notes his grandfather had taught him
options.childFeedback: Eli remembered the exact signal Grandfather taught him and blew one firm, level note to make Pip lie down.

options.text: Dropped the silver whistle into the wet clover
options.childFeedback: Eli kept the silver whistle on its leather cord and blew two more crisp notes on it in Paragraph 5—he never dropped it in the clover.

questions.provingSentenceText: Eli resisted the urge to yell across the grass.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'resisted' means stopped himself from doing something he felt like doing, because instead of yelling when Pip sped up, Eli held back and blew one firm note on the whistle.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 4, 'Instead, he blew one firm, level note' shows that Eli held back ('resisted') his habit of yelling at the puppy.
questions.retryHint: Look at the next sentence in Paragraph 4 ('Instead, he blew one firm, level note...') to see what Eli stopped himself from doing.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, why does a shepherd's whistle work better than shouting across a windy pasture?

options.text: The whistle makes a loud barking noise that scares the sheep away from the briars.
options.childFeedback: Pip's wild barking in Paragraph 1 is what scattered the sheep into the briars; the silver whistle makes smooth musical notes that keep the sheep calm.

options.text: Its magic sound puts the sheep to sleep so the shepherd can carry them into the pen.
options.childFeedback: The whistle signals the herding dog—it does not put the twenty ewes to sleep, and a boy could never carry twenty sheep into a pen!

options.text: Only adult border collies have ears strong enough to hear a human voice.
options.childFeedback: Young Pip heard Eli's shouting in Paragraph 1, but a loud human voice sounded like panic and made the puppy bark wildly.

options.text: Its clear notes travel far through the wind without sounding angry or startling the animals.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that while a loud human voice sounds like panic to a young dog and nervous sheep, a clear whistle cuts through valley wind up to half a mile away without sounding angry.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because a clear whistle cuts through valley wind without sounding angry, a working dog can hear the cue from half a mile away.
questions.childTip: Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that while a loud human voice sounds like panic to a young dog and nervous sheep, a clear whistle cuts through valley wind up to half a mile away without sounding angry.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 explains that a clear whistle cuts through valley wind without sounding angry or panicked, letting a dog hear the cue from half a mile away.
questions.retryHint: Check the last sentence of Paragraph 3 to see how a whistle sound travels through valley wind without sounding angry.

questions.prompt: How does Paragraph 5 resolve the conflict introduced in Paragraph 1?

options.text: It shows Grandfather locking Pip inside the barn while the older dog finishes all the farm chores.
options.childFeedback: Grandfather never locks Pip in the barn; he gives Eli the silver whistle so Eli and Pip can herd the sheep together.

options.text: It shows Pip obeying Eli's quiet whistle signals to guide the flock calmly through the gate instead of scattering them.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 1, Eli's shouting caused Pip to scatter the sheep into the briars, and Paragraph 5 resolves this problem when Pip obeys Eli's calm whistle notes and guides the whole flock smoothly through the gate.

options.text: It explains why sheep prefer eating clover on the hill over standing near the stone wall.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 shows the sheep walking through the open wooden gate into the pen, not debating whether clover tastes better on the hill.

options.text: It proves that ten-month-old puppies are too young to learn any herding commands.
options.childFeedback: Ten-month-old Pip obeys both whistle commands right away in Paragraph 5, proving he is smart and ready to learn.

questions.provingSentenceText: Pip rose smoothly and trotted in a wide arc around the left flank, guiding the whole flock straight through the open gate.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 1, Eli's shouting caused Pip to scatter the sheep into the briars, and Paragraph 5 resolves this problem when Pip obeys Eli's calm whistle notes and guides the whole flock smoothly through the gate.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 1, Eli's shouting and Pip's barking scattered the ewes into the briars; in Paragraph 5, Eli's calm whistle cues help Pip pause and circle wide to bring the flock smoothly through the gate.
questions.retryHint: Compare what went wrong when Eli shouted in Paragraph 1 with how Pip and the sheep respond to the whistle in Paragraph 5.

questions.prompt: Part A: Based on Paragraphs 3 through 5, why does Eli blow one long, steady blast before blowing the two short rising notes?

options.text: He wants Grandfather's older dog to run up the hill and take Pip's place.
options.childFeedback: One long blast is a command for Pip to lie flat in the grass and pause—not a call for Grandfather's older dog to take over.

options.text: He forgets the signal for circling left and blows the wrong note by mistake.
options.childFeedback: Eli does not blow the note by mistake; pausing Pip for three seconds calmed the sheep before Eli blew the two rising notes to circle left.

options.text: He needs Pip to lie down and stop his fast charge first so the sheep do not bolt in fear.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, Pip lowers his head to charge straight into the sheep, so Eli blows one long blast (the signal from Paragraph 3 to lie flat and pause) so the ewes do not bolt in fear.

options.text: One long blast tells the sheep to walk single file into the briar patch.
options.childFeedback: The whistle signals are for the border collie, not the sheep, and Eli is guiding the flock toward the open wooden gate, away from the briars.

questions.provingSentenceText: One long, steady blast told the dog to lie flat in the grass and pause.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, Pip lowers his head to charge straight into the sheep, so Eli blows one long blast (the signal from Paragraph 3 to lie flat and pause) so the ewes do not bolt in fear.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 3, one long blast means 'lie flat in the grass and pause.' When Pip lowers his head to charge the sheep in Paragraph 4, Eli blows that single long note so Pip drops into the clover and the ewes do not bolt.
questions.retryHint: Connect what Pip starts doing in Paragraph 4 ('ready to charge straight into the middle of the sheep') with what one long blast means in Paragraph 3.
